Modals for Possibility, Necessity and To Give Advice
You use modals when you want to express possibility and necessity. It can also be used to give advice.
You use may, might and could to express possibility in the past and in the future.
*Might suggests that something is less possible than may.

• might / might not + infinitive
  • could / could not + infinitive
  • may / may not + infinitive
Expressing Necessity
You use must or have to to express that something is necessarily true.

Example:
I have to bite the bullet and commit to this.
You use the modal verbs should, ought to and had better to express that they think something is a good or a bad idea.
Should is the most common way to give advice.
Passive with Modals
There are two basic patterns you use for passive modals.

modal + be + past participle
and
modal + have been + past participle
Causes and effects must be considered over and over again to make the right decision.
You ought to think on the consequences for your life.
I thought I had better speak to someone about my job prospects once I complete the course.
You must take that into consideration before you take the plunge.
Organizing Points in an Argument

You use words or phrases to organize ideas in a piece of writing.
Discourse markers show how ideas are connected. They usually come at the beginning of a sentence.
Discourse markers can show a connection to what the writer is saying and what was just written. They can also show what the writer's opinion is about what is being discussed.

Imagine you are ready for a career change. Who should you ask for advice? What should you consider?
Instructions:
Write a 10-12 line dialogue between a potential student and a college counselor about registering for a new course.
Think about the questions you would ask if you were changing careers.
Ask the counselor about a specific course or program and where to send the registration forms.
Use modals like might, may, had better and must to express possibility, necessity and whether something is a good or bad idea.
Use linking words like in addition to connect ideas.
When you have typed in ALL your answers, click the Go to Writing Task button.

Sally: Thank you for meeting me today on such short notice.
College Counselor: Happy I could squeeze you in!
Sally: I'm about to register for your Floral Arranging Diploma. I thought I had better speak to someone about my job prospects once I complete the course.
College Counselor: That's a great question. First, you might want to think seriously about this move into floristry. Designing bouquets will not make you wealthy. You must take that into consideration before you take the plunge.
Sally: I'm ready for a career change. I'm not getting the personal satisfaction out of it that I used to.

College Counselor: Also, our courses are organized into modules. There's an online component. Are you familiar with online applications?
Sally: Oh yes, I'm currently working as a journalist for Cambridge Life.
College Counselor: Perfect!
Sally: Do you think I ought to speak with a couple local florists to get their take on the industry?
College Counselor: Absolutely! You might make some new contacts.
Sally: Registration forms should be completed online, correct?

College Counselor: Your application must be sent via mail to the admissions department.
Sally: Oh, I see. I heard that it's very popular.
College Counselor: Everything is taken into account. In fact, your previous work experience can also be included with your other documents to improve your chances of admission.
Sally: Great! There might be a risk but I think it's the right option for me.
College Counselor: Indeed, everything should be considered before embarking on a new career path.
